newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Gulf Coast braces for round two with hurricane.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf Coast braces for round two with hurricane.

text.p: Coastal Louisiana residents, dazed by a surprisingly powerful punch from Hurricane Danny, began assessing damage on Friday as the Gulf Coast braced for a second round with the storm.

Danny, a minimal hurricane, swept across the tip of Louisiana on Friday, flooding highways and flattening power lines with winds gusting up to 100 miles an hour (160 kph), authorities said. No deaths or serious injuries were reported.

Hurricane warning flags were raised from Morgan City, La., east to Destin, Fla., as the eye of the nearly stationary storm drifted across Chandeleur Sound in the Gulf of Mexico with rain bands extending east to the Florida panhandle.
Mississippi Gov. Kirk Fordice issued a state of emergency but civil defence officials in coastal communities there said the main force of the storm was expected to remain offshore.

High winds and strong currents ripped an oil drilling rig from its berth and rammed it into a research vessel in Pascagoula, Miss., tearing a hole in the ship's fuel tank and spilling 500 gallons of diesel fuel into the port.
The U.S. Coast Guard secured nearby ships while state officials oversaw a hasty cleanup effort.

"We closed the port at 5 a.m., which kept a number of ships stuck at port that had wanted to get out into the harbour and ride this (storm) out," said Melody Bradley, director of the Jackson County Port Authority.
In Biloxi, Miss., Police Chief Tommy Moffett said authorities were considering opening a shelter for a large number of stranded tourists at area beaches and casinos.

"Right now, it's just a matter of trying to get ready while we wait to see if there really is anything to get ready for," he said. "We know that with hurricanes, you just never know what's going to happen. Danny could come here, head east, or turn around and go back to Louisiana."

The Copa casino in Gulfport, Miss., one of 11 floating casinos operating along the Gulf Coast, was closed for a second day on Friday but state officials decided not to order the remaining barge casinos shuttered ahead of the storm.

"It's a very difficult process to close the casinos. You have to offload and secure all of the paper money and then lock the chips and coins into vaults. They're too heavy to move so they use them for ballast," said Warren Strain, spokesman with the Mississippi Gaming Commission.

Emergency officials from Mississippi east to the Florida panhandle warned coastal residents to move to higher ground ahead of the storm but did not order mandatory evacuations. Widespread flooding was forecast from a four- to five-foot (1.2- to 1.5-metre) storm surge and up to 20 inches (51 cm) of rain forecast for coastal areas in the path of the storm in the coming days.

"The latest forecast puts landfall between Gulfport (Miss.) and Mobile (Ala.), probably early tomorrow morning," Jill Hasling, a meteorologist with private forecaster Weather Research Centre in Houston said.

High winds, steady rain and wind-driven water continued to bombard Plaquemines Parish southeast of New Orleans Friday afternoon, more than six hours after Hurricane Danny punched into the "toe" of Louisiana's boot-shaped coastline.

"I don't know how much longer we can stay ahead," Parish Council President Clyde Giordano said. "The 17 or more inches (43 cm) of rain we've already had has outpaced our ability to pump it out of the canals. I don't know what's going to happen if that storm doesn't move on off pretty soon."

About 100 boats appear to have been damaged or sunk at a large marina in Buras, La., where storm waters rose four to five feet (1.2 to 1.5 metres) within a few minutes earlier in the day. In nearby areas, house trailers were overturned, roofs blown off and trees and utility poles snapped, he said.

The crew of the fishing boat Nasty Two was riding out the storm in the captain's house of their partially sunken boat after rescuing two other fisherman from a sinking boat in the Empire deepwater canal. The Nasty Two was tossed onto rocks and itself sank in shallow water, the Coast Guard said.

West of Plaquemines, officials in Grand Isle, Louisiana's only inhabited barrier island, reported heavy damage and erosion. Most of the island's 1,530 residents obeyed a mandatory evacuation order Thursday and moved inland.
In New Orleans, the storm's impact was limited to occasional showers and wind gusts as the city was spared the heavy rains that could have caused widespread flooding.

The storm first made landfall overnight between Grand Isle and the mouth of the Mississippi River. The eye of the hurricane at 1 p.m. CDT (2 p.m. EDT) (1700 GMT) remained about 90 miles (144 km) southwest of Mobile, near latitude 29.6 north, longitude 89.1 west.
Hurricane force winds of 75 miles an hour (120 kph) extended outward about 25 miles (40 km) from the centre, with the strongest gusts on the east side of the drifting storm.
